title: Logical fallacies
examples: What is the difference between a logical fallacy and just disagreeing with someone?
Can you give me an example of the straw man fallacy in politics?
When do people usually use an ad hominem attack?

explain.say: Today we will learn about logical fallacies in arguments.

items: They make arguments seem strong but are not.
We will learn three types today.

explain.say: First we look at the ad hominem fallacy.
This fallacy attacks the person making the argument instead.

items: Person B attacks Person A's character.

explain.say: Next we study the straw man fallacy.
This fallacy misrepresents someone's argument to make it easier to attack.

items: Person B pretends A said Y.

explain.say: Finally we look at the false dilemma fallacy.

faq.q: What is the difference between a fallacy and just disagreeing?
faq.a: Disagreement is normal when people have different views. A fallacy is a specific flaw in the way an argument is built.
asks: Is it always wrong to disagree?

faq.q: Can an ad hominem attack be effective sometimes?
faq.a: While it is usually a fallacy, attacking character can sometimes reveal real issues with trust or credibility.
asks: Is it ever okay to attack someone?

faq.q: How do I spot a straw man fallacy?
faq.a: Listen carefully to what the person actually said. If the response seems exaggerated or totally different, it might be a straw man.
asks: How do I know if they are twisting my words?
What should I do when I spot this?

faq.q: Does the false dilemma mean there are no other options?
faq.a: No, it only suggests two options when many more possibilities actually exist in reality.
asks: Are there always only two choices?
Can you give another example of this?

faq.q: Which fallacy is the most common in online debates?
faq.a: All three are very common online because arguments can get heated quickly. Being aware is the best defense.
asks: Which one should I watch out for most?
Are these fallacies more common online?

facts: Ad hominem attacks target the speaker, not their argument.
The straw man fallacy involves substituting a weak argument for a strong one.
A false dilemma presents a limited set of choices when more options exist.
Identifying fallacies helps you think more critically.

quiz.say: Argument: You should not trust the scientist because he drives an old car. This is an example of:
quiz.why: It attacks the scientist's car, not his science.

wrong.0: It is a specific named fallacy, not just irrelevant.
wrong.2: This does not change the scientist's argument.
wrong.3: This does not limit the choices to two.

quiz.say: Argument: My opponent says we need better schools, but really, he just wants to waste all the school money on fancy sports fields. This is an example of:
quiz.why: It changes the opponent's call for better schools into something else.

wrong.0: It does not limit the choices to only two.
wrong.1: It is more about misrepresenting the argument than just emotion.
wrong.3: It does not attack the opponent's personal life.
